name: New Hampshire

events.title: Ratified the Constitution
events.text: New Hampshire ratified the Constitution on June 21, 1788, the 9th state to do so. The Constitution gave it 3 seats in the House until the first census.

events.title: Statewide (general ticket) elections
events.text: In the 1st through 29th Congresses (1789–1847), New Hampshire elected all of its representatives statewide on a general ticket instead of by district. This continued after the Apportionment Act of 1842 required districts, and the House seated the members anyway.

events.title: 1790 census apportionment
events.text: After the 1790 census, New Hampshire's House delegation grew from 3 to 4 seats.

events.title: 1800 census apportionment
events.text: After the 1800 census, New Hampshire's House delegation grew from 4 to 5 seats.

events.title: 1810 census apportionment
events.text: After the 1810 census, New Hampshire's House delegation grew from 5 to 6 seats.

events.title: 1820 census apportionment
events.text: After the 1820 census, New Hampshire kept 6 seats in the House.

events.title: 1830 census apportionment
events.text: After the 1830 census, New Hampshire's House delegation shrank from 6 to 5 seats.

events.title: 1840 census apportionment
events.text: After the 1840 census, New Hampshire's House delegation shrank from 5 to 4 seats.

events.title: 1850 census apportionment
events.text: After the 1850 census, New Hampshire's House delegation shrank from 4 to 3 seats.

events.title: 1860 census apportionment
events.text: After the 1860 census, New Hampshire kept 3 seats in the House.

events.title: 1870 census apportionment
events.text: After the 1870 census, New Hampshire kept 3 seats in the House.

events.title: 1880 census apportionment
events.text: After the 1880 census, New Hampshire's House delegation shrank from 3 to 2 seats.

events.title: 1890 census apportionment
events.text: After the 1890 census, New Hampshire kept 2 seats in the House.

events.text: After the 1970 census, New Hampshire kept 2 seats in the House. Because districts must have nearly equal populations, the map was redrawn with the new census counts.

events.title: Federal preclearance ends
events.text: Ten New Hampshire towns were covered by Section 5 of the Voting Rights Act, so the 2002 and 2012 congressional plans were precleared by federal officials. In 2013, a federal court in Washington, D.C., approved the state's request to end that coverage.

events.title: 2020 census apportionment
events.text: After the 2020 census, New Hampshire kept 2 seats in the House. Because districts must have nearly equal populations, the map was redrawn with the new census counts.

events.title: Court-drawn map after vetoes
events.text: The governor vetoed two legislative congressional plans on May 27, 2022. In Norelli v. Scanlan, the New Hampshire Supreme Court found the old districts unequal in population and on May 31, 2022, adopted a map that made the fewest changes needed.

compactnessNote: Polsby-Popper compactness (4π × area ÷ perimeter²) measured on the projected district shapes. It describes shape only: coastlines, rivers and county lines lower it too, so a low score is not evidence of intent. "Irregular" marks the least compact 5% of district shapes in each census era nationally.

c030.text: New Hampshire's district lines were redrawn between censuses, first used in the 1846 election. The reason has not been researched yet.

c032.text: New Hampshire's district lines were redrawn between censuses, first used in the 1850 election. The reason has not been researched yet.

c033.text: New map drawn after the 1850 census, which cut New Hampshire's seats from 4 to 3. It was first used in the 1852 election.

c048.text: New map drawn after the 1880 census, which cut New Hampshire's seats from 3 to 2. It was first used in the 1882 election.

c092.text: New Hampshire's district lines were redrawn between censuses, first used in the 1970 election. The reason has not been researched yet.

c093.text: New map drawn after the 1970 census, which left New Hampshire with 2 seats. It was first used in the 1972 election.
